disease.notes: Applies to newly sequenced non-Westernized cohorts (Ghana, Ethiopia, Tanzania). Published datasets included disease cohorts (CRC, T2D, IBD, etc.) but the primary new samples were healthy.

biomarker_name.notes: Multiple biomarkers identified across the paper related to P. copri genomic structure and functional diversity.

tumor_size_measurement.notes: No tumor measurements reported. This is a microbiome study, not an oncology clinical trial.

value: Analysis of 6,874 publicly available metagenomes from 36 datasets spanning six continents and 25 countries
1,023 P. copri genomes reconstructed (17 isolates, 1,006 metagenome-assembled genomes)
Four genetically distinct clades (A, B, C, D) with >10% inter-clade genetic divergence
P. copri began to diversify ~6.5 million years ago (clade B split)
Clade diversification occurred 3.5-2.5 million years ago, pre-dating human migration out of Africa (90-194 ka)
Ancient metagenomes analyzed from 5,300-year-old Iceman and pre-Columbian coprolites (1,300±100 BP)
New metagenomic sequencing from Ethiopia (50 metagenomes), Ghana (44 metagenomes), Tanzania (68 metagenomes), Madagascar (110 metagenomes)
Substantial functional diversity in carbohydrate metabolism between clades suggests diet-driven selection
No strong evidence that P. copri clades are associated with colorectal cancer, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, liver cirrhosis, or inflammatory bowel disease
19.2% of families showed same P. copri strain between members, suggesting possible transmission
uncurated_metadata.evidence_quote: Analysis of 6,874 publicly available metagenomes from 36 individual datasets. expanded the total number of available P. copri genomes to 1,023. four distinct clades. P. copri began to diversify ~6.5 million years ago.
uncurated_metadata.notes: Study design, scale, and key findings documented as uncurated metadata since they don't map to specific clinical outcome fields.

Paper focuses on characterizing P. copri genetic diversity via metagenomic assembly and phylogenetic analysis. The newly sequenced cohorts (Ghana, Ethiopia, Tanzania; n=162) are all healthy individuals. Disease cohort data come from re-analysis of published datasets, not primary sample collection. No participant-level clinical phenotypes reported in detail.

Age data available only at cohort level with means and ranges, not single study-level values. Ghana: 23 adults (avg 33.14 yrs, range 20–45), 25 children (avg 6.81 yrs, range 0–15); Ethiopia: 24 adults (avg 29.35 yrs, range 22–45), 26 infants (avg 1.31 yrs, range 0.167–4.5); Tanzania: 37 adults (avg 29.27 yrs, range 18–61), 31 children (avg 8.22 yrs, range 0–18).

Disease analysis performed on 10 published disease cohorts (CRC, T2D, IBD, hypertension, liver cirrhosis) but no new disease cohort data collected; reported findings were 'no strong evidence' of clade-disease association.
BMI mentioned in Methods as an analyzed variable but no values reported in Results or Tables S1–S2.
Batch 2 returned granularity='study_level', differs from batch 0 ('sample_level'); kept batch 0.
This paper is a microbial genomics and population structure study, not a clinical trial. Most clinical outcome fields (ECOG status, tumor size, overall survival) are not applicable.

Disease associations investigated (colorectal cancer, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, liver cirrhosis, IBD) showed no strong clade-level associations; author states 'no clear evidence that particular clades are associated with the subset of health conditions available for meta-analysis.'
Biomarker fields extracted represent genomic markers (genetic distances, prevalence, functional diversity) rather than traditional clinical biomarkers.
The paper does not report individual-level sample data in a tabular format suitable for per-sample extraction; all prevalence and abundance data are reported at cohort/population level.
Ancient metagenome analysis provided evolutionary context but not clinical outcome data.
